title: Define and Apply Secure Coding Guidelines and Standards
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 8: Software Development Security: Define and Apply Secure Coding Guidelines and Standards.

blocks.text: The OWASP Top 10 represents the most critical web application security risks. No standard is a guaranteed match for every organization, so these should be used as starting points from which organizations can develop and implement their own practices (a process known as tailoring).

rows: Users act outside their intended permissions
Failures in cryptography leading to data exposure
Untrusted data sent to an interpreter (SQL, OS, LDAP)
Missing or ineffective security controls in design
Default configs, unnecessary features, verbose errors
Application fetches remote resources without validation

blocks.text: OWASP has led the effort to design coding guidelines and standards for a variety of languages, software libraries, and application environments like web and mobile. The OWASP Top 10 is the most well-known output, but OWASP also provides:

items: OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) — detailed security requirements
OWASP Testing Guide — comprehensive testing methodology
OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — quick reference guides for specific security topics
OWASP Mobile Security Project — mobile-specific security guidance

blocks.text: Frameworks that automatically implement security controls (such as anti-XSS protections or CSRF tokens) should be incorporated into development practices and awareness training. Using frameworks with built-in security features is far more reliable than expecting every developer to implement security correctly from scratch. ⚠️ Exam Trap: Know the OWASP Top 10 categories at a high level. The exam is unlikely to ask about specific rankings but may present scenarios that map to these categories — especially injection, broken access control, and security misconfiguration.
The CMU Software Engineering Institute (SEI) publishes the Top 10 Secure Coding Practices (which actually contains twelve practices):

items: Validate input — validate all input from untrusted sources
Heed compiler warnings — compile code with the highest warning level and address all warnings
Architect and design for security — create a software architecture and design following security principles
Keep it simple — reduce attack surface by keeping code simple and minimizing complexity
Default deny — base access decisions on permission rather than exclusion
Adhere to the principle of least privilege — every process should operate with the minimum set of privileges
Sanitize data sent to other systems — sanitize all output sent to other systems (databases, shells, etc.)
Practice defense in depth — manage risk with multiple defensive strategies
Use effective quality assurance techniques — thorough testing helps find and eliminate vulnerabilities
Adopt a secure coding standard — develop and implement a secure coding standard for your language/platform
All input from untrusted sources must be validated — type, format, length, range, encoding
Allowlisting (whitelist) approach — define what IS allowed; reject everything else (preferred over denylisting)
Denylisting (blacklist) approach — define what IS NOT allowed; allow everything else (weaker, can be bypassed)
Validate on the server side — client-side validation can be bypassed
Parameterized queries (prepared statements) — separate code from data to prevent injection attacks
Canonicalization — convert input to a standard form before validation to prevent encoding-based bypass attacks

blocks.text: Input validation is the single most important secure coding practice. The majority of software vulnerabilities — including SQL injection, XSS, buffer overflow, and command injection — result from insufficient input validation. The allowlisting approach is strongly preferred over denylisting. With denylisting, you must anticipate every possible malicious input — and attackers are constantly finding new ways to bypass filters. With allowlisting, you define exactly what valid input looks like, and anything that doesn't match is rejected. Parameterized queries are the primary defense against SQL injection. Instead of concatenating user input into SQL strings, parameters are bound separately so the database treats them as data, not executable code. This eliminates the ability for an attacker to inject SQL commands through user input.

items: Encode output before rendering to prevent injection attacks (especially XSS)
HTML encoding — convert special characters (<, >, &, ", ') to HTML entities
URL encoding — encode special characters in URLs using percent-encoding
JavaScript encoding — escape characters that have special meaning in JavaScript
Context-specific encoding — use the right encoding for the output context (HTML body, HTML attribute, JavaScript, CSS, URL)
Fail securely — when errors occur, the system should default to a secure state (deny access, not grant it)
Do not expose sensitive information in error messages — stack traces, internal paths, database structures, version numbers
Log security-relevant events: authentication attempts, access control failures, input validation failures, application errors
Logs from application-level should be correlated with infrastructure logs for comprehensive monitoring
Data from multiple sources should be correlated to provide investigators with a holistic view of incidents
Generate strong, random session identifiers — sufficient entropy to prevent guessing
Session timeout — terminate sessions after a period of inactivity
Session invalidation — properly destroy sessions on logout (server-side, not just client-side)
Protect session tokens: HTTPS only, HttpOnly cookie flag (prevents JavaScript access), Secure cookie flag (only sent over HTTPS), SameSite attribute (prevents CSRF)
Regenerate session ID after authentication to prevent session fixation attacks
Do not expose session IDs in URLs
Language-specific secure coding standards published by Carnegie Mellon's Software Engineering Institute
Available for C, C++, Java, Perl, and Android
Provide detailed rules and recommendations organized by category (input validation, declarations, expressions, memory management, etc.)
Each rule includes: description, noncompliant code example, compliant code example, risk assessment
Organizations should adopt and tailor these standards to their specific development environment

Software and Data Integrity Failures: Code/infrastructure without integrity verification
